title: Coffee-Stained QR Scans, Yet a Clean One Fails? | So That's Why
description:
A QR Code at a drink shop gets splashed with iced coffee, yet your phone still scans it with a crisp beep. Right beside it sits a freshly printed, spotless code—only its floral border is a little too close, and no phone can read it at all. They're both grids of tiny black-and-white squares, so what makes the difference?

In this episode, Chief and Little Q trace what happens in the split second your camera scans a code: how three corner squares lock onto orientation across 360 degrees, how a two-person team measured stacks of printed flyers before the 1994 release to find the rarest black-and-white ratio, how the same math that protects deep-space probes and music CDs calculates missing data back, and why 'up to ~30% error correction' doesn't mean tearing off 30%—or why one big coffee drop and scattered tiny ink dots can have opposite fates.

Illustrations in this episode are AI-generated; all black-and-white grids shown are conceptual diagrams rather than scannable codes. Official specifications and calculation examples are listed in the references below.

p003.text: A new one next to it is clean,

p005.text: Why the gap? And why did its two inventors measure flyer lines?

p006.text: How did deep-space probe math end up inside tiny squares?

p008.text: Even wilder: one big drop beats tiny ink specks! Guess how it reads?

p009.text: When my phone reads a QR,

p011.text: If it read rigidly like books, one slight tilt would fail!

p012.text: Old supermarket 1D barcodes really do line bars up one way.

p014.text: a red laser fails unless it cuts across bars.

p015.text: Square QR Codes pack data both across and up-and-down,

p016.text: with big finder boxes in three corners!

p018.text: at any 360-degree angle, three corners tell your camera where it is!

p021.text: Think: if all four corners had identical big squares,

p022.text: spin it halfway and how could your phone find the top?

p024.text: lets phones spot up, down, left, right fast!

p025.text: Cafe tables have dark lines too—

p028.text: Before 1994's debut, Masahiro Hara's DENSO team was just two people!

p029.text: QR means Quick Response—built for speed.

p030.text: If cameras mistook nearby table lines for corners, it'd crawl!

p031.text: First: squares, rare on office forms.

p032.text: They turned piles of flyers, magazines, and boxes black and white!

p033.text: For days from dawn to night, both tallied black-to-white widths.

p034.text: Guess the rarest width ratio across all those prints?

p035.text: The rarest rhythm they found was 1 to 1 to 3 to 1 to 1!

p036.text: Slice right through a corner square: black-white-black-white-black matches it!

p038.text: hit 1-1-3-1-1 and it locks onto the QR!

p041.text: Everyday QR is Model 2, hiding a tiny alignment pattern.

p042.text: Even on a curved can, that small box aligns the grid!

p043.text: Even scanning from an angled cafe seat,

p044.text: slight perspective warp still reads fine!

p046.text: why did that clean new QR fail?

p047.text: Blame the outer white rim—officially the margin, or quiet zone!

p048.text: All four sides need a 4-module-wide blank white border!

p049.text: That floral trim ate the 4-unit margin,

p050.text: so the camera couldn't even tell where it begins!

p052.text: Then how were stained black dots saved?

p053.text: Once edges and angle lock, it reads inner black-white dots.

p054.text: Each tiny black or white dot is called a 'module'!

p056.text: each version up adds 4 modules per side.

p057.text: Biggest Version 40 reaches 177 modules per side,

p058.text: holding up to 7,089 digits or 4,296 alphanumeric characters!

p060.text: Does it copy the link three times?

p061.text: Copying it three times would waste two-thirds of the space!

p062.text: If coffee hid the copies too, it'd still fail!

p063.text: The real trick is smarter—not dot by dot,

p064.text: it packs 8 bits into one box: a 'codeword'.

p066.text: not just a single tiny dot?

p067.text: Yes, 8 bits together make one codeword box!

p068.text: Data fills boxes first, followed by math-built error-correction boxes.

p070.text: the math mentioned earlier that guards deep-space signals!

p071.text: Satellites and probes beam data from deep space;

p072.text: even through noise, this math saves lost bytes.

p073.text: Even home music CDs playing past light scratches

p076.text: no copy—how can math find it?

p077.text: Simple analogy: say you have three numbers—3, 5, and 2.

p078.text: No backup copy—just one clue beside them: they add up to 10.

p079.text: Cover the middle one: take 10 minus 3 and 2,

p080.text: and the middle one must be 5!

p081.text: Of course, the real math beats simple addition!

p082.text: Phones don't know what's dirty—how do they fix it?

p083.text: It must find BOTH which box broke AND what was inside.

p084.text: So rescuing 1 bad codeword takes 2 error-correction codewords!

p085.text: Developer DENSO WAVE shows a case:

p086.text: With 100 data boxes, to survive 50 ruined boxes,

p087.text: you add double—100 check boxes—making 200 total,

p091.text: Because dripping iced coffee won't dodge the check boxes!

p092.text: Data boxes and check boxes sit on the very same grid.

p093.text: Out of all 200 boxes, ANY 50 ruined boxes can be fixed.

p094.text: Divide by total codewords and that's 25%—matching Level Q!

p095.text: There are four levels—L, M, Q, H:

p097.text: Level Q saves about 25%, as we just saw,

p098.text: and top Level H saves about 30% of all codewords!

p100.text: can I snip off 30% with scissors?

p101.text: No scissors! Official docs say it depends on the damage—

p103.text: Plus, that percentage counts total codeword boxes,

p104.text: not 30% of paper area to tear away!

p105.text: If one tiny ink drop wrecks a corner finder square,

p106.text: your phone never spots the QR, so check boxes can't even start!

p107.text: No wonder shop QRs with a logo

p109.text: Spot on! A center logo dodges the three corners and white rim.

p110.text: Raise the error level ahead of time to pack extra check boxes,

p111.text: and your phone treats those covered center boxes

p112.text: as broken codewords, solving them back!

p114.text: Then stains hurt it much faster?

p115.text: Yes—spend quota on a logo and coffee maxes it out fast!

p116.text: Now recall our opening riddle: same total stain area—

p117.text: one big coffee puddle vs scattered tiny ink dots—which lives?

p120.text: Just the opposite! Remember: 8 bits count as ONE whole box!

p121.text: Reed-Solomon's smallest unit is one whole codeword box.

p122.text: Dirty 1 bit in a box or wreck all 8 bits—either way,

p123.text: the decoder's ledger marks '1 broken codeword box'!

p124.text: Official docs note it excels at concentrated burst damage!

p125.text: Coffee pooled over 2 boxes breaks just 2 boxes—easy save.

p126.text: Scatter specks like pepper into 8 boxes—1 dot per box—

p127.text: 8 boxes break at once, blowing the quota!

p129.text: and the whole quota is gone!

p131.text: why not set every QR to H?

p132.text: Check boxes take real estate too—no free lunch!

p133.text: In a fixed grid, more check boxes leave less room for data.

p134.text: Take smallest Version 1: Level L fits up to 41 digits;

p135.text: crank it to Level H and capacity drops to 17 digits!

p136.text: Say you want to encode 50 digits:

p137.text: Version 2 M fits it, while Version 2 H holds only 34!

p138.text: To keep Level H for 50 digits, you jump to Version 3—

p139.text: growing to 29 by 29 modules to fit!

p140.text: On the same tiny cup-sleeve sticker, denser dots shrink super thin;

p141.text: slight ink bleed or hand shake makes it harder to scan!

p144.text: Right! Oily factories pick Q or H;

p145.text: clean spots with huge data pick Level L.

p146.text: Daily menus mostly pick balanced 15% Level M.

p147.text: Now look back at those two cafe QRs—see it?

p148.text: Got it! On that coffee-stained QR,

p149.text: iced coffee missed the 3 corners and margin!

p151.text: while floral trim ate the border—unfindable!

p152.text: Nailed it! Three corners, alignment, and quiet zone lock position;

p153.text: then Reed-Solomon check boxes rebuild the gap.

p154.text: On your next cup or receipt QR,

p155.text: check its white border and spot the tiny alignment box!
